candidates.quote: Perhaps all the dragons in our lives are princesses who are only waiting to see us act, just once, with beauty and courage.
candidates.author: Rainer Maria Rilke
candidates.whyThisMonth: It tells a reader who is dreading the day that the thing waiting for them may be asking for courage rather than threatening them with it.

candidates.quote: It is not in the still calm of life, or the repose of a pacific station, that great characters are formed.
candidates.author: Abigail Adams
candidates.whyThisMonth: A mother writing to a boy of twelve says plainly that the hard stretch is the making of him, which is the whole argument of the month in one sentence.

candidates.quote: Do you not see how necessary a World of Pains and troubles is to school an Intelligence and make it a soul?
candidates.author: John Keats
candidates.work: letter to George and Georgiana Keats
candidates.locator: the journal letter of 14 February to 3 May 1819, the entry of 21 April
candidates.whyThisMonth: It gives trouble a job to do instead of a meaning to find, which is easier to carry at six in the morning than consolation is.

candidates.quote: I’m a pessimist because of intelligence, but an optimist because of will.
candidates.author: Antonio Gramsci
candidates.whyThisMonth: It lets a reader keep a clear view of how bad things are and still get up, because the getting up is a decision and not a forecast.

candidates.quote: In spite of everything I still believe that people are really good at heart.
candidates.author: Anne Frank
candidates.work: The Diary of a Young Girl
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous sentence written under trial in the last century, and it is a choice about other people rather than a report on them.

candidates.quote: Never measure the height of a mountain until you have reached the top. Then you will see how low it was.
candidates.author: Dag Hammarskjöld
candidates.translator: Leif Sjöberg and W. H. Auden, 1964
candidates.whyThisMonth: For the morning when the size of the thing ahead is the problem: it says the size is not knowable yet, so start climbing.

candidates.quote: I can’t do much with my hands; so I will make a battering-ram of my head and make a way through this rough-and-tumble world.
candidates.author: Louisa May Alcott
candidates.work: Life, Letters, and Journals, ed. Ednah D. Cheney
candidates.locator: the journal for 1850, Roberts Brothers edition of 1889
candidates.whyThisMonth: A teenager with no money and no standing decides what she will use instead, which is the cheerful end of courage rather than the grim end.

candidates.quote: I will not be ‘famous’, ‘great’. I will go on adventuring, changing, opening my mind and my eyes, refusing to be stamped and stereotyped.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.work: A Writer’s Diary, ed. Leonard Woolf
candidates.locator: entry of 29 October 1933, Hogarth Press edition of 1953
candidates.whyThisMonth: The trial here is other people’s opinion of you, and the courage is the daily refusal to be fixed by it.

candidates.quote: There is a stubbornness about me that never can bear to be frightened at the will of others. My courage always rises at every attempt to intimidate me.
candidates.author: Jane Austen
candidates.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
candidates.whyThisMonth: Courage in a drawing room and not on a battlefield, which is where most readers will need it before nine o’clock.

candidates.quote: I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will.
candidates.author: Charlotte Brontë
candidates.locator: vol. II, ch. 8 (ch. 23), in the orchard at Thornfield
candidates.speaker: Jane Eyre
candidates.whyThisMonth: A governess with nothing on her side states what she is, and a reader can borrow the sentence whole on a morning when they feel caught.

candidates.quote: I wanted you to see what real courage is, instead of getting the idea that courage is a man with a gun in his hand. It’s when you know you’re licked before you begin but you begin anyway and you see it through no matter what.
candidates.author: Harper Lee
candidates.locator: ch. 11, to Jem after Mrs Dubose
candidates.speaker: Atticus Finch
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the month’s definition: courage is not the odds improving, it is beginning anyway, and a reader can test the day against it.

candidates.quote: Hope cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist. It is just like roads across the earth. For actually the earth had no roads to begin with, but when many men pass one way, a road is made.
candidates.author: Lu Xun
candidates.locator: the closing lines, Selected Stories of Lu Hsun, 1960
candidates.whyThisMonth: It hands hope back as something made by walking, which is the only version of it that survives a hard week.

candidates.quote: The unknown, the unforetold, the unprovable, that is what life is based on. Ignorance is the ground of thought. Unproof is the ground of action.
candidates.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
candidates.locator: ch. 5, The Domestication of Hunch, at Otherhord
candidates.speaker: Faxe
candidates.whyThisMonth: For the reader who wants to know how it turns out before they will move: it says not knowing is the ground you act from, not an obstacle to acting.

candidates.quote: The virtue of prosperity is temperance; the virtue of adversity is fortitude; which in morals is the more heroical virtue.
candidates.author: Francis Bacon
candidates.work: Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
candidates.whyThisMonth: It ranks the two seasons of a life and puts the hard one first, so a reader in the hard one is not merely enduring but practising the better virtue.

candidates.quote: Your silence will not protect you.
candidates.author: Audre Lorde
candidates.locator: the essay The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action, Crossing Press edition of 1984
candidates.whyThisMonth: Six words that remove the safest excuse for not speaking, on a morning when someone is deciding whether to say the hard thing.

candidates.quote: What saves a man is to take a step. Then another step. It is always the same step, but you have to take it.
candidates.author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
candidates.locator: the chapter Prisoner of the Sand
candidates.whyThisMonth: The smallest possible instruction for a day that looks too big, from a man who walked out of a desert on exactly that rule.
